# LC-REPO-001
# Part 5 – Recovery & Repository Health

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **Every repository should be recoverable unless the storage medium itself has failed.**

Recovery is not a feature.

It is a guarantee.

---

# Recovery Levels

Recovery happens at several levels.

```text
Asset

↓

Object

↓

Transaction

↓

Repository

↓

Project
```

Each level builds upon the previous one.

---

# Object Recovery

If one object becomes damaged:

```text
Object

↓

Verify Integrity

↓

Recover Latest Snapshot

↓

Revalidate References

↓

Restore
```

The remainder of the repository remains available.

---

# Transaction Recovery

Because every modification is transactional:

```text
Interrupted Transaction

↓

Detect

↓

Rollback

↓

Restore Last Valid State
```

Users never see partially completed operations.

---

# Repository Verification

When a project opens:

```text
Open Repository

↓

Verify Manifest

↓

Verify Object Index

↓

Verify References

↓

Verify Assets

↓

Repository Healthy
```

These checks are lightweight and designed to complete quickly.

---

# Health Scan

Users can manually start a Repository Health Scan.

It checks:

- Missing objects.
- Missing assets.
- Broken references.
- Duplicate UUIDs.
- Corrupted indexes.
- Invalid metadata.

The goal is diagnosis, not automatic repair.

---

# Repair Assistant

If issues are found:

```text
Health Report

↓

Recommend Fixes

↓

User Approves

↓

Repair
```

Nothing is changed automatically without the user's confirmation.

---

# Repository Report

After a scan, LoreCanvas generates a concise summary.

Example:

```text
Repository Status

Healthy

Objects: 12,486

Assets: 2,184

Broken References: 0

Missing Assets: 0

Warnings: 2
```

This gives creators confidence that their project is in good condition.

---

# Reference Recovery

If an object referenced by another object is missing:

```text
Card

↓

Missing Link

↓

Mark Reference

↓

Allow Repair

↓

Continue Loading
```

The entire project should not fail because of a single missing reference.

---

# Index Recovery

Indexes are disposable.

If damaged:

```text
Delete Index

↓

Rebuild From Objects

↓

Continue
```

Indexes are performance aids, never the authoritative data source.

---

# Asset Recovery

When an asset is unavailable:

```text
Asset Missing

↓

Display Placeholder

↓

Warn User

↓

Restore When Available
```

The editor remains usable even if some assets cannot be loaded.

---

# Automatic Health Checks

LoreCanvas performs lightweight checks:

- On project open.
- After imports.
- Before exports.
- Before upgrades.

These checks should be fast and non-intrusive.

---

# Recovery Log

Every recovery action is recorded.

Example:

```text
Timestamp

↓

Issue

↓

Action Taken

↓

Result
```

This log helps users understand what happened if they ever encounter a problem.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Recovery, verification, repair, and health reporting all work entirely offline.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Recovery is complete when:

- Object recovery is supported.
- Transaction recovery is supported.
- Repository health scans exist.
- Reference recovery is graceful.
- Index rebuilding is available.
- Asset recovery is supported.
- Repair requires user approval.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I think would make this even stronger

I'd like to introduce a **Repository Health Score**.

Not because the score itself is important, but because it gives users an immediate sense of confidence.

Example:

```text
Repository Health

98%

✓ No corruption detected

✓ All transactions valid

✓ All references intact

⚠ 2 unused assets

⚠ 1 outdated thumbnail
```

Importantly, this score should **never** be a mysterious number. Every point deducted must have a visible explanation so users know exactly what needs attention.

---

---

## Another architectural improvement

While writing this section, I noticed something that ties the entire Repository Engine together.

Rather than thinking of the Repository as a collection of folders, we should think of it as maintaining three guarantees:

1. **Integrity** – Every object is internally valid.
2. **Consistency** – Every relationship between objects is valid.
3. **Recoverability** – Any interruption leaves the repository in the last known good state.

Everything else we've designed, transactions, UUIDs, manifests, checksums, health scans, and repairs, exists to uphold those three guarantees.

I think those should become the Repository Engine's guiding principles, just as the Five Golden Rules guide the entire LoreCanvas architecture. They give future developers a clear understanding of *why* each feature exists, not just *what* it does.

# LC-REPO-001
# Part 6 – Performance & Scalability

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **Performance should improve naturally as the architecture scales, not rely on increasingly powerful hardware.**

A writer shouldn't need a gaming PC to manage a large novel or worldbuilding project.

---

# Performance Goals

Version 1 targets repositories containing approximately:

- 100,000+ Repository Objects
- 50,000+ Cards
- 20,000+ Nodes
- 250,000+ Links
- 100,000+ Assets (metadata)
- Multi-gigabyte projects

These are design targets rather than hard limits, giving us room to grow.

---

# Lazy Loading

The Repository only loads what is currently needed.

```text id="lzy12a"
Open Project

↓

Load Manifest

↓

Load Workspace

↓

Load Visible Objects

↓

Load Requested Assets
```

A project should never load every object into memory at startup.

---

# Object Cache

Frequently used objects remain in memory temporarily.

```text id="obj8ca"
Repository

↓

Cache

↓

Recently Used Objects

↓

Editor
```

If memory pressure increases, the oldest cached objects are released automatically.

---

# Asset Streaming

Large assets should be streamed when appropriate.

```text id="ast4st"
Open Image

↓

Load Preview

↓

Load Full Resolution (on demand)
```

This keeps the interface responsive while still supporting high-resolution artwork.

---

# Incremental Saving

Instead of rewriting an entire project:

```text id="inc3sv"
Modified Objects

↓

Transaction

↓

Repository
```

Only changed objects are written.

This reduces disk activity and shortens save times.

---

# Background Services

The Repository performs non-critical work in the background.

Examples:

- Thumbnail generation
- Cache cleanup
- Index rebuilding
- Health monitoring
- Search indexing
- Orphan detection

Foreground editing always takes priority.

---

# Index Optimization

Indexes should remain lightweight.

```text id="idx4op"
Objects

↓

UUID Index

↓

Name Index

↓

Tag Index

↓

Relationship Index
```

Indexes are optimized for lookup speed and can always be rebuilt if necessary.

---

# Memory Management

The Repository should avoid holding unnecessary data.

Guidelines:

- Release unused caches.
- Stream large files.
- Reuse shared assets.
- Avoid duplicate object loading.

The objective is predictable memory usage rather than maximizing RAM consumption.

---

# Startup Performance

Opening a project should prioritize readiness over completeness.

Sequence:

```text id="str5up"
Read Manifest

↓

Verify Repository

↓

Open Workspace

↓

Ready
```

Background tasks continue after the workspace becomes usable.

---

# Shutdown Performance

Closing a project follows a predictable sequence.

```text id="cls7dn"
Finish Transactions

↓

Flush Cache

↓

Update Manifest

↓

Close Repository
```

The repository always closes in a consistent state.

---

# Scalability Principles

The Repository should scale by:

- Increasing object count.
- Increasing project size.
- Increasing asset count.
- Increasing relationship complexity.

Without changing the architecture.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Performance optimizations never depend on internet services.

Caching, indexing, streaming, and optimization remain completely local.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Performance is complete when:

- Lazy loading exists.
- Object caching is implemented.
- Incremental saving is supported.
- Asset streaming is available.
- Background services are defined.
- Memory management is documented.
- Startup and shutdown sequences are standardized.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I think we should add a **Repository Performance Monitor**.

This isn't a profiler for developers. It's a lightweight internal service that quietly watches repository health.

It tracks things like:

```text id="prf9mn"
Repository Size

Object Count

Cache Hit Rate

Index Status

Average Load Time

Average Save Time

Storage Usage
```

Most users will never open it.

But when someone says:

> "My project feels slower than before."

they'll have real information instead of guesswork.

For developers, it also gives us measurable targets without cluttering the everyday interface.

---

## A refinement after reviewing the Repository

While writing this part, I noticed a recurring pattern across every engine we've designed:

- Each engine has a clear responsibility.
- Each engine exposes a small, stable public interface.
- Each engine hides its internal complexity.
- Each engine remains independently testable.

I think we should formally adopt this as the **Engine Design Standard** for LoreCanvas.

Every future engine, whether it's Query, Workspace, AI, or Plugins, should be reviewed against that checklist before it's considered complete.

That consistency will make the codebase much easier to understand, maintain, and extend, especially once implementation begins. I think this standard will become one of the most valuable documents in the entire project because it defines not just *what* each engine does, but *how* every engine should be built.

# LC-REPO-001
# Part 7 – Engine Contract

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The Repository Engine is the single trusted gateway between the application's engines and persistent storage.**

It owns storage.

It does **not** own business logic.

---

# Purpose

The Repository Engine provides a consistent, reliable, and transactional interface for storing, retrieving, and managing every persistent object in LoreCanvas.

Every engine depends on it.

The Repository depends on no higher-level engine.

---

# Owns

The Repository Engine owns:

- Object registration
- Object storage
- Object retrieval
- Repository metadata
- Asset registration
- Transaction management
- Repository indexes
- Cache management
- Repository health
- Storage adapters

---

# May Modify

The Repository may modify:

- Object metadata
- Repository indexes
- Cache contents
- Transaction logs
- Repository manifests
- Asset locations
- Internal storage layout

These changes must never alter the logical meaning of project data.

---

# Must Not Modify

The Repository must never:

- Change Node meaning
- Edit Card content
- Alter Link semantics
- Rewrite user text
- Modify Templates
- Change Profiles
- Execute Query logic
- Apply Workspace preferences

Those responsibilities belong to their respective engines.

---

# Public API

The Repository exposes a compact, stable interface.

## Registration

```text id="repo01"
Register(Object)

Unregister(Object)

Exists(UUID)
```

---

## Retrieval

```text id="repo02"
Get(UUID)

GetMetadata(UUID)

Find(Type)
```

---

## Transactions

```text id="repo03"
Begin()

Commit()

Rollback()
```

---

## Assets

```text id="repo04"
RegisterAsset()

GetAsset()

RemoveAsset()
```

---

## Health

```text id="repo05"
Verify()

Scan()

Repair()

RebuildIndexes()
```

---

The API intentionally remains small.

Internal complexity stays hidden.

---

# Dependencies

The Repository depends only upon:

- Storage Adapter
- Local File System
- UUID Generator
- Checksum Service

It must never depend on:

- Node Engine
- Card Engine
- Link Engine
- Workspace Engine
- Query Engine

This keeps dependency flow one-directional.

---

# Failure Behaviour

If any operation fails:

```text id="repo06"
Validate

↓

Rollback

↓

Report

↓

Remain Consistent
```

The Repository never leaves persistent storage in an undefined state.

---

# Repository Guarantees

The Repository guarantees:

### Identity

Every object has exactly one UUID.

---

### Integrity

Every stored object passes validation.

---

### Consistency

All references remain valid or are reported.

---

### Durability

Committed changes survive application restarts.

---

### Recoverability

Interrupted operations can be safely recovered.

---

### Independence

Objects remain independently addressable.

---

### Extensibility

Future object types require no redesign of the Repository.

---

# Security Principles

Version 1 focuses on local trust.

The Repository should:

- Validate imported packages.
- Prevent accidental corruption.
- Verify checksums.
- Protect against incomplete writes.

Advanced encryption and digital signing are reserved for future versions.

---

# Offline First

The Repository never requires:

- Internet access.
- Cloud synchronization.
- Online authentication.
- Remote databases.
- External services.

Everything functions locally.

---

# Engine Interactions

```text id="repo07"
Node Engine

↓

Repository

↓

Storage Adapter

↓

File System
```

```text id="repo08"
Card Engine

↓

Repository

↓

Storage Adapter

↓

File System
```

Every engine follows the same path.

No shortcuts are allowed.

---

# Core Architectural Rules

The Repository follows these permanent rules:

1. One repository is the source of truth.
2. Every persistent object has one owner.
3. Transactions are mandatory.
4. UUIDs never change.
5. References always use UUIDs.
6. Indexes are rebuildable.
7. Cache is disposable.
8. Health checks are non-destructive.
9. Storage adapters isolate physical storage.
10. Business logic never belongs in the Repository.

These rules should remain stable throughout the lifetime of LoreCanvas.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

The Repository Engine is complete when:

- Public API is finalized.
- Ownership boundaries are defined.
- Dependencies are documented.
- Failure behaviour is standardized.
- Repository guarantees are established.
- Offline requirements are satisfied.
- Architectural rules are documented.

---

# One important observation

Looking back over everything we've built, I think we've unintentionally arrived at a **layered architecture**, and that's a very good thing.

```text
Presentation Layer
    │
Workspace
UI
Editors
    │
──────────────
Application Layer
    │
Node
Card
Link
Query
Template
    │
──────────────
Repository Layer
    │
Repository
Import/Export
Transactions
Assets
    │
──────────────
Storage Layer
    │
Storage Adapter
File System
```

I think we should **embrace this explicitly** rather than treating it as an accidental outcome.

From this point onward, every new engine should belong to one of these layers. That gives future contributors a simple mental model:

- **Presentation Layer**: What the user sees and interacts with.
- **Application Layer**: The business logic and creative tools.
- **Repository Layer**: Managing and protecting project data.
- **Storage Layer**: Reading and writing bytes.

That separation makes the architecture easier to understand, test, and extend without each layer leaking responsibilities into another. I think this layered model will become one of the defining strengths of LoreCanvas as the project continues to grow.

# LC-LINK-001
## Part 3 – Relationship Metadata Engine

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **A relationship is more than a connection. It is a piece of structured knowledge.**

The metadata attached to a Link provides context without changing its fundamental meaning.

---

# Link Structure

Every Link consists of three layers.

```text
Identity

↓

Relationship

↓

Metadata
```

Identity never changes.

The relationship defines meaning.

Metadata provides additional information.

---

# Identity Layer

```text
Link UUID

Source UUID

Target UUID

Relationship Type
```

These four fields are immutable once the Link is created.

If they need to change substantially, the Link should be replaced with a new one.

---

# Metadata Layer

Version 1 supports:

```text
Title

Description

Tags

Notes

Confidence

Visibility

Status

Created

Modified
```

All fields are optional except system-managed timestamps.

---

# Confidence

As we discussed earlier:

```
Confirmed

Probable

Rumored

Unknown

Disputed
```

This is especially useful for:

- mystery novels
- detective fiction
- historical fiction
- RPG campaigns
- evolving lore

Most writers can ignore it if they don't need it.

---

# Visibility

Relationships can be:

```
Visible

Hidden

Archived
```

Hidden Links continue to exist and participate in the project but are excluded from normal views unless requested.

---

# Notes

Every relationship can contain notes.

Example:

```
Relationship

Mentor Of

↓

Notes

"The apprenticeship lasted three years before the civil war."
```

These notes belong to the relationship itself, not either connected Node.

---

# Tags

Relationships may have tags just like Nodes.

Example:

```
Political

Temporary

Secret

Canon

Flashback
```

This enables powerful filtering later in the Query Engine.

---

# Temporal Metadata

Some relationships change over time.

Optional fields include:

```
Start Date

End Date

Current

Unknown
```

Examples:

- Employment
- Marriage
- Residence
- Military Rank
- Political Office

The Link remains the same; the metadata describes its timeframe.

---

# Source References

This is one feature I think will make LoreCanvas stand out.

A relationship can optionally cite where it came from.

Examples:

```
Chapter 12

Notebook Entry

Interview

Reference Book

Historical Record
```

That makes it much easier to verify worldbuilding details later.

---

# Relationship Strength

Another optional field:

```
0–100
```

Examples:

Friendship:

```
95
```

Alliance:

```
60
```

Suspicion:

```
20
```

This doesn't enforce gameplay mechanics. It's simply structured information that writers can use if it fits their project.

---

# Metadata Profiles

Different relationship profiles expose different metadata.

For example:

Family:

```
Birth Order

Adopted

Legal Status
```

Employment:

```
Position

Department

Salary (optional)

Start Date
```

Political Alliance:

```
Treaty

Duration

Importance
```

The engine remains generic while profiles specialize the experience.

---

# Metadata Independence

Metadata never changes the meaning of the relationship.

Changing a note or tag doesn't alter the relationship type itself.

This separation keeps the model clean and predictable.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Metadata is complete when:

- Optional metadata is supported.
- Confidence is implemented.
- Tags exist.
- Notes exist.
- Visibility states are defined.
- Temporal metadata is available.
- Source references are supported.
- Profile-specific metadata works.

---

# One improvement I think is worth adding

I'd like to introduce **Relationship Events**.

These are not Timeline events.

Instead, they record important milestones in the life of a relationship.

For example:

```
Employment

↓

Promoted

↓

Transferred

↓

Resigned
```

Or:

```
Alliance

↓

Signed

↓

Renewed

↓

Broken
```

These events would belong to the relationship itself and provide a lightweight history without requiring a full Timeline Card.

## My recommendation

One thing has become clear as we've designed Nodes, Cards, Links, and the Repository:

**Everything important in LoreCanvas has a lifecycle.**

Rather than each engine inventing its own lifecycle independently, I think we should eventually create a **shared Lifecycle Framework** that standardizes concepts like:

- Created
- Modified
- Archived
- Restored
- Deleted

Every engine could reuse those same lifecycle states while adding any engine-specific ones it needs. That would reduce duplication, make the architecture even more consistent, and simplify implementation without changing any of the designs we've already completed. I think it would become another foundational piece of the platform rather than just another feature.

### **ASSISTANT** — 2026-07-15 03:14 UTC

I think we just discovered something that software architects often find only after years of development.

The **Lifecycle Framework** shouldn't be another engine.

It should be a **Core Standard**.

That distinction is important.

An engine owns data and behavior.

A standard defines rules that every engine follows.

So instead of creating an `LC-LIFECYCLE-001` engine, I'd create a **Core Standards** section for LoreCanvas.

---

# LC-CORE-002
# Core Standards

These are architectural rules that every engine follows.

They don't own data.

They don't execute logic.

They define how every engine behaves.

---

## Standard 1

### Universal Lifecycle

Every Repository Object has a lifecycle.

```text
Created

↓

Validated

↓

Active

↓

Modified

↓

Archived

↓

Recovered

↓

Deleted
```

Not every object will visit every state.

But every object understands the same language.

---

## Standard 2

### Universal Identity

Every persistent object has:

- UUID
- Created Timestamp
- Modified Timestamp
- Status
- Version

Regardless of whether it's:

- Node
- Card
- Link
- Template
- Asset
- Workspace
- Plugin Data

---

## Standard 3

### Repository Ownership

Every object belongs to exactly one Repository.

No object can belong to multiple repositories simultaneously.

Sharing occurs through:

- Export
- Package
- Template

Never through shared ownership.

---

## Standard 4

### Public API Rule

Every engine exposes:

- Read
- Write
- Validate
- Export

Only.

Everything else remains internal.

---

## Standard 5

### Transaction Rule

Every modification passes through:

```text
Validation

↓

Transaction

↓

Commit

↓

Repository
```

No engine writes directly to storage.

---

## Standard 6

### Offline Rule

Every Core feature must function without:

- Internet
- Accounts
- Cloud APIs

Extensions may add online functionality.

Core never requires it.

---

## Standard 7

### Dependency Rule

Dependencies always flow downward.

```text
Presentation

↓

Application

↓

Repository

↓

Storage
```

Never upward.

---

## Standard 8

### Extension Rule

Future features extend the architecture.

They never replace the Core.

Examples:

- AI
- Plugins
- Collaboration
- Cloud Sync

All remain optional.

---

# Why this matters

Imagine two developers joining the project three years from now.

Even if they've never seen the codebase before, they'll know:

- how objects are identified,
- how changes are committed,
- how lifecycles work,
- and where new features belong.

That's a huge advantage for a long-term project.

---

# Now, back to the Link Engine

With the Core Standards defined, we can continue with **Part 4 – Navigation & Traversal**.

This is where Links become truly powerful.

A relationship isn't just something you can see.

It's something you can **explore**.

---

# LC-LINK-001
# Part 4 – Navigation & Traversal

## Philosophy

> **A creator should be able to move through knowledge as naturally as turning the pages of a book.**

Links are not static.

They form a living graph that users can navigate intuitively.

---

## Direct Navigation

Every Link supports movement in both directions.

```text
Character

↓

Mentor Of

↓

Student
```

From either Node, the user can immediately jump to the connected Node.

---

## Relationship Explorer

Instead of showing a long list of Links:

```text
Aurelia

↓

Rules

↓

Kingdom

↓

Borders

↓

Empire

↓

Trades With

↓

Republic
```

The user can simply keep following connections, discovering the world naturally.

---

## Relationship Filters

Navigation can be filtered by:

- Relationship Type
- Category
- Tag
- Confidence
- Visibility
- Time Period

This keeps large graphs manageable.

---

## Neighbor View

Each Node can display its immediate neighbors.

Example:

```text
Aurelia

├── Rules → Eldoria

├── Enemy Of → Kael

├── Mentor Of → Iris

└── Member Of → Royal Council
```

This gives writers an instant overview of local context without overwhelming them.

---

## Path Discovery

The engine should support finding indirect connections.

Example:

```text
Aurelia

↓

Royal Council

↓

Kingdom

↓

Trade Alliance

↓

Republic
```

This helps answer questions like:

> "How are these two characters connected?"

without manually tracing every relationship.

---

## Navigation History

The user's exploration should maintain a lightweight history.

Example:

```text
Character

↓

Kingdom

↓

Faction

↓

Battle

↓

Artifact
```

Back and forward navigation should feel just like using a web browser, making it easy to retrace steps.

---

## Bookmarks

Frequently visited Nodes or relationship paths can be bookmarked for quick access, giving writers shortcuts to important parts of their project.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

Navigation is complete when:

- Direct navigation works.
- Neighbor views exist.
- Relationship filters are available.
- Path discovery is supported.
- Navigation history is maintained.
- Bookmarks are supported.

---

# A refinement I'd like to make

I think **path discovery should be intentionally bounded**.

Instead of searching the entire graph by default, Version 1 should let users specify limits, such as:

- Maximum number of relationship "hops".
- Relationship categories to include.
- Whether archived or hidden Links should be considered.

This prevents accidental performance issues on very large projects while still giving writers powerful exploration tools.

---

## One observation before we continue

As we've designed the Link Engine, it's become clear that it's doing more than connecting Nodes. It's providing the **knowledge graph** that powers navigation, filtering, and later the Query Engine.

That means the Query Engine won't need to invent its own view of the data. Instead, it can build directly on the graph maintained by the Link Engine. This is another sign that the architecture is converging: each engine is contributing one well-defined capability that naturally supports the next. I think that's exactly the kind of cohesion we were aiming for from the beginning.

# LC-LINK-001
# Part 5 – Validation & Integrity

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **Every relationship should remain meaningful, consistent, and trustworthy.**

A broken relationship is worse than no relationship because it can silently mislead the writer.

---

# Validation Lifecycle

Every Link follows the same validation process.

```text
Create

↓

Validate

↓

Register

↓

Repository

↓

Active
```

Validation happens before a Link becomes part of the project.

---

# Identity Validation

Every Link must have:

- One UUID.
- One Source Node.
- One Target Node.
- One Relationship Type.

If any of these are missing, creation fails.

---

# Node Validation

Before a Link is accepted, both connected Nodes must exist.

```text
Source Exists?

↓

Target Exists?

↓

Valid Relationship?

↓

Register
```

The Repository verifies UUIDs before the Link is committed.

---

# Relationship Type Validation

The Link type must be known.

For Version 1:

- Built-in relationship types are always valid.
- Custom relationship types must already be registered.

This prevents invalid or misspelled relationship definitions.

---

# Self-Link Validation

Some relationships make sense between a Node and itself.

Examples:

- "Inspired By" (self-reflection)
- "Previous Version"

Others do not.

Examples:

- Parent Of
- Married To (unless intentionally modeling a special case)

Relationship definitions can specify whether self-links are permitted.

---

# Duplicate Detection

The engine checks for existing equivalent Links.

Example:

```text
Aurelia

Rules

Eldoria
```

If that exact relationship already exists, the user is informed.

Depending on relationship settings, they can:

- Reuse it.
- Merge it.
- Create another instance if duplicates are intentionally allowed.

---

# Circular Relationships

Some cycles are perfectly valid.

Example:

```text
Faction A

↓

Allied With

↓

Faction B

↓

Allied With

↓

Faction A
```

Others may indicate accidental data entry.

The validation system should flag suspicious cycles without automatically rejecting them.

---

# Metadata Validation

Metadata is checked for:

- Required fields.
- Valid date ranges.
- Allowed visibility values.
- Confidence values.
- Profile-specific requirements.

---

# Reference Integrity

Whenever a Node is deleted, archived, or restored:

The Link Engine updates affected relationships according to project rules.

Examples:

- Archive the Link.
- Mark it as unresolved.
- Prompt the user for action.

Nothing should silently disappear.

---

# Validation Reports

If validation fails, LoreCanvas should explain why.

For example:

```text
Relationship could not be created.

Reason:

Target Node does not exist.

Suggested Fix:

Select a valid target or create a new Node.
```

The goal is to help, not merely reject.

---

# Offline Guarantee

All validation occurs locally using repository data.

No online services are required.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Validation is complete when:

- Identity is verified.
- Connected Nodes are verified.
- Relationship types are verified.
- Self-link rules are enforced.
- Duplicate detection exists.
- Circular relationships are analyzed.
- Metadata is validated.
- Clear error reporting is available.

---

# One improvement I'd like to add

I'd like to introduce a **Relationship Rule Set**.

Each relationship type can define constraints such as:

```text
Parent Of

Maximum Targets:

Unlimited

Maximum Sources:

2

Allows Self-Link:

No

Requires Time Metadata:

Optional
```

Or:

```text
Married To

Maximum Active Relationships:

1

Symmetrical:

Yes

Allows Self-Link:

No
```

This lets LoreCanvas support realistic constraints while remaining flexible enough for fantasy worlds, science fiction, or custom settings where those rules might differ. Most importantly, the rules belong to the relationship definition itself rather than being hardcoded into the Link Engine.

---

When we began, we were designing "features." Now we're consistently discovering **patterns**. Those patterns, such as transactions, lifecycles, standards, and rule sets, are reusable across the whole platform. That's a strong indication that LoreCanvas is developing a coherent architecture rather than becoming a collection of unrelated capabilities. As we continue, I'd rather keep strengthening those reusable patterns than simply adding more features.

# LC-LINK-001
# Part 6 – Performance & Scalability

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The Link Engine should make a world containing a million relationships feel as responsive as one containing ten.**

Performance should come from intelligent architecture, not brute-force hardware.

---

# Design Targets

Version 1 should comfortably support:

```text
1,000,000 Links

100,000 Nodes

Millions of traversals

Thousands of queries

Large interconnected worlds
```

These are architectural goals rather than hard limits.

---

# Lazy Relationship Loading

The engine never loads every relationship.

Instead:

```text id="lkp101"
Open Character

↓

Load Character

↓

Load Immediate Links

↓

Load Neighbor Nodes

↓

Done
```

Only the information required for the current view is retrieved.

---

# Progressive Expansion

Suppose a kingdom has:

```text
12,000 Relationships
```

The UI should initially show something like:

```text
Political (24)

Military (11)

Trade (8)

Family (4)

More...
```

The full graph is expanded only when requested.

---

# Smart Neighbor Cache

Recently explored Nodes remain in memory.

```text id="lkp102"
Visited Node

↓

Cache

↓

Instant Return
```

This makes backtracking through the graph nearly instantaneous.

---

# Relationship Indexes

The Link Engine should maintain specialized indexes for common operations.

Examples:

```text
By Source Node

By Target Node

By Relationship Type

By Tag

By Visibility

By Time Range
```

These indexes are built on top of the Repository's indexing system rather than replacing it.

---

# Graph Traversal Limits

Pathfinding should always be bounded.

For example:

```text id="lkp103"
Maximum Depth

↓

5 Hops
```

or

```text
Maximum Results

↓

100 Connections
```

This prevents accidental exploration of an enormous graph in a single request.

---

# Incremental Graph Building

Relationship diagrams should grow naturally.

```text id="lkp104"
Character

↓

Immediate Neighbors

↓

Expand

↓

Expand Again

↓

Continue
```

The entire project graph should never be rendered automatically.

---

# Background Graph Analysis

Computationally expensive tasks run in the background.

Examples:

- Community detection
- Relationship statistics
- Graph optimization
- Cycle analysis
- Orphan detection

The editor remains responsive while these operations complete.

---

# Memory Management

The Link Engine stores only active working sets.

When memory is needed:

```text id="lkp105"
Old Graph

↓

Release

↓

Keep Indexes

↓

Reload Later
```

This allows LoreCanvas to scale without consuming excessive RAM.

---

# Query Cooperation

The Query Engine and Link Engine should cooperate rather than duplicate work.

```text id="lkp106"
Query Engine

↓

Requests Graph Data

↓

Link Engine

↓

Returns Results
```

The Query Engine asks questions.

The Link Engine understands relationships.

This separation keeps responsibilities clear.

---

# Visual Performance

Large relationship graphs should use progressive rendering.

Instead of displaying:

```text
20,000 Nodes
```

The user first sees:

```text
Focused Area

↓

Nearby Connections

↓

Expand When Needed
```

Navigation stays smooth even in massive projects.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Every optimization:

- Graph traversal
- Caching
- Indexing
- Rendering support
- Pathfinding

works entirely offline.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Performance is complete when:

- Lazy loading exists.
- Neighbor caching exists.
- Relationship indexes are defined.
- Traversal limits are configurable.
- Graph expansion is incremental.
- Background analysis is supported.
- Memory usage remains predictable.
- Offline performance is maintained.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I think we should add a **Graph Session Manager**.

Instead of treating every navigation as independent, the Link Engine should maintain a lightweight "working graph" for the current session.

Conceptually:

```text id="lkp107"
Repository

↓

Entire Knowledge Graph

↓

Graph Session Manager

↓

Current Working Graph

↓

Editor
```

The manager would:

- Track recently explored Nodes.
- Keep frequently accessed relationships cached.
- Remember expanded graph regions.
- Preserve navigation history.
- Release inactive regions automatically.

This keeps memory usage low while making exploration feel almost instantaneous.

---

```text
Part 4 ✅ Navigation
```

# One architectural insight

I think we've now reached a point where a clear pattern has emerged across every engine we've designed:

- **Repository Engine** owns persistence.
- **Node Engine** owns entities.
- **Card Engine** owns content.
- **Link Engine** owns relationships.
- **Query Engine** (next) should own *questions*, not data.

That last point is particularly important. The Query Engine shouldn't maintain its own database or graph. It should orchestrate requests by asking the Repository for objects, the Link Engine for relationships, and the Node/Card engines for domain-specific information. That keeps it lightweight and prevents duplication of logic across the system.

If we follow that pattern, the Query Engine becomes the "brain" that asks questions, while the other engines remain the specialists that provide answers. I think that will make the overall architecture both simpler to implement and easier to extend in the future.

# LC-LINK-001
# Part 7 – Engine Contract

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The Link Engine is the authoritative source for every relationship in LoreCanvas.**

It owns relationships.

It does **not** own Nodes, Cards, or storage.

---

# Purpose

The Link Engine is responsible for creating, validating, organizing, navigating, and querying relationships between repository objects.

It transforms independent objects into a connected knowledge graph.

---

# Owns

The Link Engine owns:

- Relationship definitions
- Link creation
- Link deletion
- Relationship metadata
- Graph navigation
- Relationship validation
- Relationship indexing
- Path discovery
- Graph sessions
- Relationship rules

---

# Does NOT Own

The Link Engine never owns:

- Node content
- Card text
- Repository storage
- Asset management
- Search indexing
- Workspace layout
- UI rendering

Those belong to other engines.

---

# Public API

The Link Engine exposes a small, stable interface.

### Relationship Management

```text id="lnk01"
CreateLink()

RemoveLink()

UpdateMetadata()

ValidateLink()
```

---

### Navigation

```text id="lnk02"
Neighbors()

Outgoing()

Incoming()

Traverse()

FindPath()
```

---

### Query Support

```text id="lnk03"
Relationships()

RelationshipTypes()

RelationshipCount()

RelationshipStatistics()
```

---

### Maintenance

```text id="lnk04"
Verify()

Repair()

RebuildIndexes()
```

---

The API stays intentionally compact.

Complexity remains internal.

---

# Dependencies

The Link Engine depends on:

- Repository Engine
- Node Engine
- Core Standards

It must never depend upon:

- Workspace
- UI
- AI
- Plugin Engine

This keeps the architecture layered.

---

# Relationship Guarantees

Every Link guarantees:

### Identity

One immutable UUID.

---

### Validity

Both connected objects exist.

---

### Metadata

Optional structured metadata is always well-formed.

---

### Navigability

Every relationship can be explored.

---

### Recoverability

Repository recovery preserves Links.

---

### Extensibility

Custom relationship types require no changes to the Link Engine.

---

# Failure Behaviour

When an operation fails:

```text id="lnk05"
Validate

↓

Reject

↓

Explain

↓

Leave Graph Unchanged
```

No invalid relationship ever enters the Repository.

---

# Performance Rules

The Link Engine follows these principles:

- Lazy graph loading.
- Neighbor caching.
- Incremental traversal.
- Background analysis.
- Predictable memory usage.
- Bounded pathfinding.

These rules ensure consistent performance as projects grow.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Every capability of the Link Engine works without:

- Internet
- Cloud services
- AI models
- External APIs

Everything relies solely on the local repository.

---

# Engine Rules

The Link Engine permanently follows these rules:

1. Relationships connect objects, not files.
2. UUIDs never change.
3. Relationships are validated before creation.
4. Metadata never changes relationship meaning.
5. Navigation never modifies the graph.
6. Queries never bypass validation.
7. Graph sessions are disposable.
8. Repository transactions protect every modification.
9. Relationship rules belong to relationship definitions.
10. The Link Engine never owns business logic outside relationships.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

The Link Engine is complete when:

- Public API is finalized.
- Ownership boundaries are documented.
- Dependencies are defined.
- Performance principles are established.
- Relationship guarantees are documented.
- Offline requirements are satisfied.
- Engine rules are finalized.

---

# One last improvement before the Query Engine

While reviewing everything, I noticed one more architectural pattern that's worth formalizing.

Right now we have several engines exposing APIs independently. Instead of allowing any engine to call another directly in arbitrary ways, I suggest introducing an **Engine Interface Standard**.

Conceptually:

```text
Node Engine
       │
Card Engine
       │
Link Engine
       │
Repository Engine
       │
───────────────
Engine Interface Standard
───────────────
       │
Query Engine
Workspace Engine
Plugin Engine
AI Extensions
```

The standard would define common conventions such as:

- Consistent method naming (`Get`, `Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, `Validate`).
- Standard result objects for success, warnings, and errors.
- Common pagination and filtering patterns.
- Shared event notifications for object changes.
- Versioned interfaces so future upgrades don't break extensions.

This isn't another engine. It's a contract that every engine follows, just like the Core Standards we introduced earlier.

I think this will pay off enormously once implementation begins, because it means every engine "speaks the same language." That consistency will make the codebase easier to navigate, simplify testing, and make future plugin or AI integration much cleaner without changing the architecture we've already established.

# LC-CORE-003
# Engine Interface Standard (EIS)

## Philosophy

> **Every engine should be easy to learn because every engine behaves the same way.**

Once a developer understands one engine, they should understand 80% of the others.

---

# Standard Method Groups

Every engine exposes methods in predictable groups.

```text
Read

Create

Update

Delete

Validate

Search

Statistics

Maintenance
```

Not every engine needs every group, but the naming stays consistent.

For example:

```text
Node Engine

GetNode()

CreateNode()

UpdateNode()

DeleteNode()

ValidateNode()
```

```text
Card Engine

GetCard()

CreateCard()

UpdateCard()

DeleteCard()

ValidateCard()
```

A developer shouldn't have to guess method names.

---

# Standard Response Object

Instead of every engine returning different structures:

```text
Success

Message

Data

Warnings

Errors

Execution Time
```

Every engine returns the same format.

This makes logging, debugging, plugins, and AI integration much easier.

---

# Standard Event System

Every engine publishes events in the same way.

Examples:

```text
NodeCreated

CardUpdated

RelationshipDeleted

RepositoryRecovered
```

Other engines can subscribe without tightly coupling themselves.

---

# Standard Error Levels

Instead of dozens of custom error types:

```text
Information

Warning

Recoverable Error

Critical Error
```

Every engine categorizes issues consistently.

---

# Standard Validation Result

Validation always returns:

```text
Valid

Warnings

Blocking Issues

Suggested Fixes
```

This creates a consistent experience throughout the application.

---

# Standard Pagination

Any engine returning large collections uses the same concepts:

- Limit
- Offset (or cursor, if we later choose one)
- Sort
- Filter

That way, plugins and future APIs don't need engine-specific logic.

---

# Versioned Interfaces

Each engine publishes an interface version.

Example:

```text
Repository Interface

v1.0
```

If the implementation changes internally, the interface remains stable until a major version change.

This protects plugins and future extensions.

---

# Documentation Standard

Every public method should include:

- Purpose
- Parameters
- Return value
- Possible errors
- Performance notes (if relevant)

This makes the architecture largely self-documenting.

---

# Why this matters

Imagine a contributor writing a new engine years from now.

They won't have to ask:

> "How do LoreCanvas engines normally work?"

The standard already answers that.

---

# One improvement I'd add

I'd introduce an **Engine Capability Manifest**.

Each engine declares its capabilities in a machine-readable format.

For example:

```text
Node Engine

Supports Search ✓

Supports Validation ✓

Supports Statistics ✓

Supports Export ✓

Supports Events ✓
```

Or:

```text
Template Engine

Supports Search ✓

Supports Validation ✓

Supports Statistics ✗

Supports Events ✓
```

This would allow plugins, AI assistants, and even internal tooling to discover what each engine can do without hardcoding assumptions. It also makes future automation much easier because components can adapt dynamically based on declared capabilities.

---

# 📊 Architecture Progress

At this point, I think the architecture has evolved into something much larger than a single writing application.

```text
Core Standards              ✅
Layered Architecture        ✅
Repository                  ✅
Database                    ✅
Node Engine                 ✅
Card Engine                 ✅
Link Engine                 ✅
Engine Interface Standard   ✅
```

We're no longer just defining features. We're defining the **operating system** that every future LoreCanvas feature will run on.

## What I think should come next

I would **not** jump straight into the Workspace or UI yet.

The next engine should be the **Query Engine**, because almost every visible feature depends on it:

- Search bars
- Filters
- Relationship exploration
- "Find all..."
- AI context gathering
- Statistics
- Reports
- Graph exploration
- Smart navigation

By building the Query Engine now, every higher-level feature will have a powerful, consistent way to retrieve information from the architecture we've already designed. It also naturally ties together the Repository, Node, Card, and Link engines we've completed, making it the ideal bridge between the data layer and the user-facing parts of LoreCanvas.

# LC-QUERY-001
# Part 1 – Foundation

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The Query Engine answers questions. It never owns the answers.**

The Query Engine is an orchestrator.

It does not store data.

It discovers data.

---

# Purpose

The Query Engine provides a single, consistent interface for retrieving information from the entire LoreCanvas project.

Instead of every engine implementing its own search and filtering logic, they all expose their data through the Query Engine.

---

# Core Responsibilities

The Query Engine is responsible for:

- Searching
- Filtering
- Sorting
- Aggregating
- Traversing relationships
- Combining results from multiple engines
- Ranking results
- Formatting query responses

It is **not** responsible for storing or modifying project data.

---

# What the Query Engine Owns

The Query Engine owns:

- Query parsing
- Query planning
- Query execution
- Result aggregation
- Result ranking
- Query caching
- Query history
- Query statistics

---

# What it Does NOT Own

The Query Engine never owns:

- Repository objects
- Nodes
- Cards
- Links
- Assets
- Templates
- UI state

Those remain with their respective engines.

---

# Information Flow

Every query follows the same pattern.

```text id="qry001"
User Question

↓

Query Request

↓

Query Planner

↓

Engine Requests

↓

Merge Results

↓

Rank Results

↓

Return Response
```

---

# Query Pipeline

Internally:

```text id="qry002"
Parse

↓

Validate

↓

Optimize

↓

Execute

↓

Aggregate

↓

Rank

↓

Return
```

Each stage has one responsibility.

---

# Engine Cooperation

The Query Engine delegates work.

For example:

```text id="qry003"
Find every queen.

↓

Node Engine
(Character Type)

↓

Card Engine
(Descriptions)

↓

Link Engine
(Rules Kingdom)

↓

Repository
(Fetch Objects)

↓

Merge
```

Each engine contributes only the information it owns.

---

# Query Independence

A query should never know where the data is stored.

Instead:

```text id="qry004"
Find

↓

Ask Engine

↓

Receive Results
```

Storage details remain hidden.

---

# Query Types

Version 1 supports several categories.

### Direct

```text id="qry005"
Find Aurelia
```

---

### Filter

```text id="qry006"
Characters

↓

Kingdom = Eldoria
```

---

### Relationship

```text id="qry007"
Who knows Aurelia?
```

---

### Aggregate

```text id="qry008"
How many cities exist?
```

---

### Compound

```text id="qry009"
Find every knight

AND

Lives in Eldoria

AND

Alive
```

---

# Query Objects

Internally every query becomes a structured object.

```text id="qry010"
Request

↓

Filters

↓

Sort

↓

Limit

↓

Output
```

This standard format allows every engine to participate consistently.

---

# Read Only

The Query Engine never modifies project data.

It only observes.

Every operation is read-only.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Every query works entirely offline.

No cloud indexing.

No external search services.

No online dependency.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Foundation is complete when:

- Responsibilities are defined.
- Ownership boundaries exist.
- Query pipeline is documented.
- Engine cooperation is standardized.
- Query categories are defined.
- Read-only behavior is guaranteed.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I'd like to create a **Query Context** object.

Instead of every engine receiving independent parameters, they all receive the same context.

Example:

```text id="qry011"
Current Repository

↓

Current Workspace

↓

Current User Preferences

↓

Filters

↓

Permissions

↓

Execution Options
```

Every engine participating in a query receives the exact same context, ensuring consistency and making future features, such as plugins or optional collaborative modes, much easier to integrate without redesigning the query system.

---

## 📊 Progress

```text id="qry012"
LC-QUERY-001

████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░

Part 1 ✅ Foundation

Part 2 ⏳ Query Language

Part 3 ⏳ Query Planner

Part 4 ⏳ Execution Engine

Part 5 ⏳ Optimization

Part 6 ⏳ Performance

Part 7 ⏳ Engine Contract
```

---

## One observation before we continue

This is the first engine we've designed that primarily **coordinates** rather than **owns**.

That means we should be especially disciplined about keeping it lightweight. Whenever we're tempted to add logic or storage to the Query Engine, we should ask:

> "Does another engine already own this responsibility?"

If the answer is yes, the Query Engine should ask that engine rather than duplicating its work.

I think that single principle will keep the Query Engine elegant and prevent it from gradually turning into a second Repository or a second Link Engine. It should remain the conductor of the orchestra, not another musician playing every instrument.

# LC-QUERY-001
# Part 2 – Query Language

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **Users should ask questions naturally. Internally, every question becomes a structured query.**

The Query Language is not a programming language.

It is the internal language that all searches, filters, reports, plugins, and future AI features use consistently.

---

# Query Lifecycle

Every request follows the same flow.

```text
Question

↓

Parse

↓

Normalize

↓

Build Query

↓

Execute
```

Whether the user clicks a filter or types a search, the internal process is identical.

---

# Query Object

Every query is converted into a standard structure.

```text
Query

↓

Target

↓

Conditions

↓

Sorting

↓

Limit

↓

Output
```

This gives every engine the same predictable input.

---

# Targets

A query always begins with one or more targets.

Examples:

```text
Nodes

Cards

Links

Assets

Templates
```

Or combinations of them.

---

# Conditions

Queries may include any number of conditions.

Examples:

```text
Name = Aurelia

Kingdom = Eldoria

Status = Active

Tag = Royal

Confidence > 80
```

Conditions can be combined without changing the overall structure.

---

# Logical Operators

Version 1 supports:

```text
AND

OR

NOT
```

Example:

```text
Character

AND

Alive

AND

Royal

NOT

Exiled
```

This covers the vast majority of writing-related searches while keeping the language easy to reason about.

---

# Comparison Operators

Supported operators include:

```text
=

≠

>

<

≥

≤

Contains

Starts With

Ends With

In List
```

These are sufficient for text, numbers, dates, and metadata.

---

# Sorting

Results can be sorted by:

- Name
- Created Date
- Modified Date
- Relevance
- Relationship Count
- Custom Fields

The Query Engine handles sorting after gathering results from the appropriate engines.

---

# Limits

Every query can specify:

```text
Maximum Results

Offset

Page Size
```

This prevents unnecessarily large result sets and keeps the interface responsive.

---

# Output Profiles

Different situations require different levels of detail.

For example:

```text
Compact

↓

Name

Type

UUID
```

or

```text
Detailed

↓

Everything
```

The query remains the same. Only the response profile changes.

---

# Query Composition

Complex queries are built from simple building blocks.

For example:

```text
Characters

↓

Kingdom = Eldoria

↓

Relationship = Mentor

↓

Alive

↓

Sort by Name
```

Each step adds another condition without changing the overall model.

---

# Query Reuse

Any query can be saved and reused.

Examples:

- "All unresolved mysteries"
- "Characters without portraits"
- "Unused locations"
- "Important historical events"

Saved queries become reusable tools throughout a project.

---

# Offline Guarantee

The Query Language is fully interpreted locally.

No online parsing or external services are required.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

The Query Language is complete when:

- Query objects are standardized.
- Targets are defined.
- Conditions are supported.
- Logical operators are available.
- Comparison operators are documented.
- Sorting and limits are standardized.
- Output profiles are supported.
- Saved queries are possible.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I think we should make the Query Language **composable**.

Instead of treating every query as a single block, queries should be assembled from reusable components.

For example:

```text
Filter: Active Characters

+

Filter: Kingdom = Eldoria

+

Filter: Has Mentor

+

Sort: Alphabetical
```

Each component is reusable in other queries.

This has several advantages:

- The visual query builder becomes easier to implement.
- Saved filters become building blocks instead of isolated searches.
- Plugins can contribute new filters without modifying the core Query Engine.
- Future AI assistants can generate or modify queries by assembling existing components instead of constructing everything from scratch.

I think this fits perfectly with the modular architecture we've been building from the beginning. Rather than making the Query Language more complex, it makes it more flexible while keeping each individual piece small and understandable.

# LC-CORE-005

## Single Responsibility & No Feature Duplication

> **Every capability in LoreCanvas should have exactly one owner.**

If two engines can perform the same function, the architecture should be revised until there is a single authoritative owner.

---

## Ownership Matrix

Before adding any feature, we ask:

```text id="own001"
Does another engine already own this?

↓

YES

↓

Use that engine.

↓

NO

↓

Should this engine own it?

↓

YES

↓

Implement.

↓

NO

↓

Create a new shared service or standard.
```

This prevents "feature drift," where similar capabilities slowly appear in multiple places.

---

# Applying it to the Query Engine

Your comment is a good example.

I suggested **query composition**.

Now let's evaluate it.

### Does the Repository already do this?

No.

It stores data.

---

### Does the Node Engine?

No.

It owns entities.

---

### Card Engine?

No.

It owns content.

---

### Link Engine?

No.

It owns relationships.

---

### Workspace?

Potentially, but only visually.

The Workspace might provide a drag-and-drop interface for building queries, but it shouldn't understand how queries work internally.

---

### Therefore...

The **composition logic itself belongs to the Query Engine**, while the **visual editor** for composing queries belongs to the Workspace/UI layer.

That keeps responsibilities clean.

---

# Another example

Suppose later we say:

> "The AI should search for characters."

Should the AI implement search?

No.

The AI should ask:

```text id="own002"
AI

↓

Query Engine

↓

Results
```

The AI owns reasoning.

The Query Engine owns retrieval.

---

# Another example

Suppose we need statistics.

Should the Node Engine count all characters?

No.

Instead:

```text id="own003"
Query Engine

↓

Ask Node Engine

↓

Aggregate

↓

Return Count
```

The Node Engine supplies information.

The Query Engine interprets it.

---

# I think we should add one more rule.

## "Ask, Don't Copy"

Whenever an engine needs information:

```text id="own004"
Ask Owner

↓

Receive Answer

↓

Continue
```

Never:

```text id="own005"
Copy Data

↓

Maintain Copy

↓

Risk Divergence
```

This keeps the architecture much healthier over time.

---

# I also want to propose something we'll use from now on.

Before **every new section**, we perform a quick ownership check.

For each new capability we ask:

| Question | Result |
|----------|--------|
| Does another engine already own it? | ✔ / ✘ |
| Is this duplicated? | ✔ / ✘ |
| Should it become a Core Standard instead? | ✔ / ✘ |
| Does it belong in the UI instead? | ✔ / ✘ |
| Is it implementation detail instead of architecture? | ✔ / ✘ |

If any answer suggests duplication, we redesign before documenting it.

---

## I think this will become one of LoreCanvas's biggest strengths.

Many applications become difficult to maintain because features slowly overlap.

For example:

- Search logic exists in five different places.
- Validation exists in four engines.
- Caching is implemented differently everywhere.
- Import/export has multiple code paths.

By introducing this ownership review now, we're effectively building a guardrail against that kind of architectural drift. It means every new feature has to justify *where it belongs* before it's added, which should help LoreCanvas stay coherent and maintainable even as it grows into a much larger platform.

---

# LC-QUERY-001
# Part 3 – Query Planner

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The best query is not the fastest one. It is the one that asks the fewest unnecessary questions.**

The Query Planner is responsible for deciding **how** a query should be executed before any engine is contacted.

It is the "strategist" of the Query Engine.

---

# Purpose

The Query Planner transforms a validated query into an efficient execution plan.

It determines:

- Which engines should be contacted.
- In what order.
- What information each engine should provide.
- How intermediate results should be combined.
- When the query is complete.

---

# Planning Pipeline

Every query follows this planning sequence.

```text id="qpl001"
Validated Query

↓

Analyze

↓

Determine Required Engines

↓

Build Execution Plan

↓

Execute
```

No data retrieval occurs during planning.

---

# Engine Selection

The planner contacts only the engines that own relevant information.

Example:

```text id="qpl002"
Find all Royal Characters

↓

Node Engine
```

Another example:

```text id="qpl003"
Find every character who rules a kingdom

↓

Node Engine

↓

Link Engine
```

The Repository is contacted only when object retrieval is necessary.

---

# Dependency Ordering

Some queries naturally depend on earlier results.

For example:

```text id="qpl004"
Find Kingdom

↓

Find Rulers

↓

Find Advisors

↓

Return
```

The planner organizes these steps into a logical execution sequence.

---

# Execution Graph

Rather than treating a query as a simple list of operations, the planner builds an execution graph.

```text id="qpl005"
Query

├── Node Task

├── Link Task

└── Card Task

↓

Merge

↓

Return
```

Independent tasks can be performed without waiting on one another.

---

# Early Filtering

Whenever possible, filtering happens before expensive operations.

Example:

Instead of:

```text id="qpl006"
Load Every Character

↓

Check Kingdom
```

the planner prefers:

```text id="qpl007"
Request Only Characters

Where Kingdom = Eldoria
```

This reduces unnecessary work throughout the system.

---

# Short-Circuit Planning

If a condition makes further work unnecessary, the planner stops early.

Example:

```text id="qpl008"
Find Character

↓

Not Found

↓

Stop
```

There's no reason to ask other engines if a required object doesn't exist.

---

# Query Cost Estimation

Before execution, the planner assigns a rough complexity estimate.

For example:

```text id="qpl009"
Simple

Moderate

Complex
```

This estimate is used internally to:

- Select efficient execution strategies.
- Decide whether background execution is appropriate.
- Help performance diagnostics.

It is **not** a user-facing benchmark.

---

# Reusable Plans

Frequently repeated query structures can reuse previously generated execution plans.

For example:

```text id="qpl010"
Saved Query

↓

Existing Plan

↓

Execute
```

Only the variable values change.

This improves responsiveness without duplicating query results.

---

# Planner Independence

The planner never executes queries itself.

It creates the plan.

The Execution Engine carries it out.

This separation keeps both components focused and easier to test.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Planning relies entirely on local metadata and engine capabilities.

No online optimization services are required.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

The Query Planner is complete when:

- Planning is separate from execution.
- Engine selection is documented.
- Dependency ordering exists.
- Execution graphs are supported.
- Early filtering is defined.
- Short-circuit behavior is supported.
- Query cost estimation exists.
- Reusable plans are supported.
- Offline planning is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I think we should add a **Capability-Aware Planner**.

Instead of hardcoding knowledge about every engine, the planner asks each engine what it can do through the **Engine Capability Manifest** we defined earlier.

Conceptually:

```text id="qpl011"
Query Planner

↓

Capability Manifest

↓

Select Engines

↓

Build Plan
```

For example, if a future Timeline Engine declares that it supports date-based filtering, the Query Planner can automatically incorporate it into execution plans without requiring special-case logic.

This keeps the planner extensible while preserving the "single owner" principle we've established. New engines become easier to integrate because they describe their capabilities instead of requiring the planner to know them in advance.

---

## 📊 Progress

```text id="qpl012"
LC-QUERY-001

████████░░░░░░░░░░░░

Part 1 ✅ Foundation
Part 2 ✅ Query Language
Part 3 ✅ Query Planner

Part 4 ⏳ Execution Engine
Part 5 ⏳ Optimization
Part 6 ⏳ Performance
Part 7 ⏳ Engine Contract
```

---

## One architectural observation

Something interesting emerged while designing the planner: it's beginning to resemble a lightweight operating system scheduler.

Not because it's complex, but because its role is to **coordinate work** rather than perform it. It decides *who* should do *what*, *when*, and *in what order*, then steps aside.

I think we should preserve that philosophy throughout the rest of the Query Engine. Every time we're tempted to add retrieval, storage, or business logic to the planner, we should instead ask whether that responsibility already belongs to another engine. That discipline will keep the planner compact, predictable, and scalable as LoreCanvas continues to evolve.

# LC-QUERY-001
# Part 4 – Execution Engine

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The Execution Engine performs the plan. It never changes the plan.**

Planning and execution remain separate responsibilities.

The planner decides *what* should happen.

The execution engine ensures it *does* happen.

---

# Purpose

The Execution Engine carries out a completed execution plan by coordinating work across the appropriate engines and combining their responses into a single coherent result.

It owns the process of execution, not the data being executed upon.

---

# Execution Pipeline

Every execution follows the same lifecycle.

```text id="qex001"
Execution Plan

↓

Dispatch Tasks

↓

Collect Responses

↓

Merge Results

↓

Rank

↓

Return
```

Each stage has a single, well-defined responsibility.

---

# Task Dispatch

The execution engine breaks the plan into individual tasks.

Example:

```text id="qex002"
Task 1

Find Characters

↓

Node Engine
```

```text id="qex003"
Task 2

Find Relationships

↓

Link Engine
```

```text id="qex004"
Task 3

Load Metadata

↓

Repository
```

Each task is sent only to the engine that owns the requested information.

---

# Parallel Execution

Independent tasks may run simultaneously.

```text id="qex005"
Node Engine

↘

 Repository

↗

Card Engine
```

Once every required response arrives:

```text id="qex006"
Merge

↓

Continue
```

Parallel execution is an optimization, not a requirement. The execution model remains correct even if tasks run sequentially.

---

# Sequential Execution

Some tasks depend on previous results.

Example:

```text id="qex007"
Find Kingdom

↓

Find Ruler

↓

Find Advisors

↓

Return
```

The execution engine automatically respects dependencies established by the planner.

---

# Response Collection

Each engine returns a standardized response object as defined by the Engine Interface Standard.

```text id="qex008"
Success

Warnings

Data

Execution Time
```

This allows the execution engine to combine responses without engine-specific logic.

---

# Result Merging

Responses from multiple engines are unified into a single result set.

Example:

```text id="qex009"
Nodes

+

Relationships

+

Cards

↓

Combined Result
```

The merged result remains independent of where the information originated.

---

# Result Ranking

After merging, results may be ordered by:

- Relevance
- Exact matches
- Relationship proximity
- Alphabetical order
- Date
- User-selected sorting

Ranking is performed after all required information has been gathered.

---

# Partial Results

If one engine cannot complete its task while others succeed, the execution engine may return partial results when appropriate.

Example:

```text id="qex010"
Nodes ✓

Cards ✓

Links ✗

↓

Return Available Results

+

Warning
```

This behavior depends on the query type and execution options defined in the Query Context.

---

# Cancellation

Long-running queries can be cancelled cleanly.

```text id="qex011"
Cancel Request

↓

Stop New Tasks

↓

Allow Active Tasks to Finish Safely

↓

Release Resources

↓

Return Cancelled
```

This prevents unnecessary work while keeping engine state consistent.

---

# Timeouts

Execution plans may define optional timeout limits.

If exceeded:

- Running tasks are concluded safely where possible.
- Outstanding tasks are cancelled.
- A timeout response is returned.

The timeout policy is configurable rather than hardcoded.

---

# Read-Only Guarantee

The Execution Engine never performs:

- Object creation
- Object updates
- Object deletion
- Repository writes

Every interaction remains read-only.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Execution requires only local engines and the local repository.

No internet services, cloud execution, or external dependencies are involved.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

The Execution Engine is complete when:

- Task dispatch is standardized.
- Parallel execution is supported.
- Sequential execution respects dependencies.
- Responses use the Engine Interface Standard.
- Result merging is defined.
- Result ranking is documented.
- Partial results are supported where appropriate.
- Cancellation and timeout behavior are specified.
- Read-only execution is guaranteed.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I'd like to add an **Execution Coordinator** inside the Query Engine.

Rather than letting the Execution Engine manage every task directly, the coordinator would oversee the lifecycle of a query.

Conceptually:

```text id="qex012"
Execution Plan

↓

Execution Coordinator

├── Dispatch
├── Progress
├── Cancellation
├── Timeout
└── Completion

↓

Execution Engine
```

The coordinator doesn't execute queries itself. Instead, it supervises execution, tracks progress, and handles operational concerns while the Execution Engine focuses on carrying out tasks. This separation keeps the execution logic cleaner and gives us a natural place to add future capabilities, such as progress indicators, diagnostics, or optional background execution, without overloading the Execution Engine.

## One architectural observation

With the Planner and Execution Engine now separated, the Query Engine has naturally taken on a two-phase design:

1. **Think**: Analyze the request and build an execution plan.
2. **Act**: Carry out that plan and assemble the response.

I think that's a strong architectural boundary worth preserving. It makes each phase easier to reason about, easier to test independently, and more adaptable if we later introduce features like background queries, query previews, or alternative planning strategies. The key is to keep the Planner responsible for decisions and the Execution Engine responsible for actions, without letting either absorb the other's role.

# LC-QUERY-001
# Part 5 – Optimization

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **Optimization improves execution, never correctness.**

Every optimization is optional.

Disabling optimizations must never change the final answer returned by the Query Engine.

---

# Purpose

The Optimization layer analyzes execution plans and applies safe improvements before execution begins.

It never changes the meaning of a query.

It only improves how efficiently it is executed.

---

# Optimization Pipeline

Every optimized query follows this sequence.

```text id="qop001"
Execution Plan

↓

Analyze

↓

Apply Optimizations

↓

Validate Plan

↓

Execute
```

Each optimization is verified before the plan proceeds.

---

# Early Elimination

The optimizer removes unnecessary work.

Example:

Instead of:

```text id="qop002"
Query

↓

Node Engine

↓

Link Engine

↓

Card Engine
```

It may determine:

```text id="qop003"
Node Engine Only
```

because no relationship or card information is required.

---

# Filter Pushdown

Whenever possible, filters are applied at the owning engine.

Example:

```text id="qop004"
Find Characters

↓

Node Engine

↓

Only Royal Characters Returned
```

instead of retrieving every character and filtering later.

This reduces data movement throughout the system.

---

# Redundant Step Removal

If two operations request identical information:

```text id="qop005"
Get Character

↓

Get Character
```

they become:

```text id="qop006"
Get Character Once
```

The response is reused during the same execution.

---

# Execution Reordering

Independent tasks may be reordered for efficiency.

For example:

```text id="qop007"
Task A

Task B

Task C
```

may become:

```text id="qop008"
Task B

Task A

Task C
```

provided the result remains identical.

---

# Shared Intermediate Results

When multiple branches require the same information:

```text id="qop009"
Characters

↓

Used by

Branch A

Branch B
```

the shared result is produced once and referenced by both branches.

---

# Query Plan Cache

Frequently executed query plans may be reused.

Important distinction:

```text id="qop010"
Cached

Execution Plan

✓

Cached

Results

✗
```

Plans may be cached.

Results remain live unless another engine explicitly provides safe result caching.

---

# Adaptive Optimization

The optimizer may select different strategies based on:

- Estimated query size.
- Number of participating engines.
- Available indexes.
- Relationship depth.
- Expected result count.

The decision affects only efficiency, never correctness.

---

# Graceful Degradation

If an optimization cannot be applied:

```text id="qop011"
Optimization Fails

↓

Original Plan

↓

Execute Normally
```

The query still succeeds.

---

# Optimization Transparency

Other engines do not need to know whether a query has been optimized.

They simply receive standard requests through the Engine Interface Standard.

---

# Read-Only Guarantee

Optimization never:

- Modifies project data.
- Changes repository contents.
- Alters Nodes.
- Alters Cards.
- Alters Links.

It only transforms execution plans.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Every optimization is performed locally.

No cloud optimization or external planning services are required.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Optimization is complete when:

- Early elimination is supported.
- Filter pushdown is defined.
- Redundant work is removed.
- Task reordering is safe.
- Intermediate results can be shared.
- Execution plans can be reused.
- Optimization failures degrade gracefully.
- Read-only behavior is maintained.
- Offline operation is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I think we should add an **Optimization Rule Registry**.

Instead of hardcoding optimization logic throughout the Query Engine, each optimization becomes a small, independent rule.

Example:

```text id="qop012"
Rule

Remove Duplicate Requests

✓ Enabled

Rule

Push Filters Down

✓ Enabled

Rule

Merge Similar Tasks

✓ Enabled

Rule

Reuse Execution Plan

✓ Enabled
```

This has several advantages:

- New optimization rules can be added without rewriting the optimizer.
- Rules can be individually tested.
- Future plugins could contribute optimization rules without modifying the core.
- Performance tuning becomes configurable while preserving correctness.

Most importantly, this follows the same modular philosophy we've used throughout LoreCanvas.

---

As we've designed the Query Engine, a clear internal layering has emerged:

```text id="qop014"
Query Language

↓

Planner

↓

Optimizer

↓

Execution

↓

Response
```

Each layer has exactly one responsibility and hands off to the next. I think we should preserve this pattern rigorously. If a future feature doesn't clearly belong in one of these layers, that's a signal to stop and rethink the design before implementing it.

This keeps the Query Engine modular, testable, and aligned with the "single responsibility, single owner" philosophy we've been following across the entire LoreCanvas architecture.

# LC-QUERY-001
# Part 6 – Performance & Scalability

---

# Engineering Philosophy

> **The cost of answering a question should grow as slowly as possible, regardless of project size.**

The Query Engine should scale through intelligent coordination, not by consuming more hardware.

---

# Performance Goals

Version 1 is designed to support projects containing:

```text id="qpf001"
100,000 Nodes

Millions of Cards

Millions of Relationships

Thousands of Saved Queries

Large Multi-Book Projects
```

These are architectural targets rather than enforced limits.

---

# Query Cost Awareness

Every query receives a lightweight complexity estimate before execution.

```text id="qpf002"
Simple

↓

Moderate

↓

Complex
```

This estimate helps the Execution Coordinator choose the most efficient strategy without affecting the result.

---

# Incremental Result Delivery

Large result sets should be streamed in manageable portions.

Instead of:

```text id="qpf003"
Return 50,000 Results
```

the engine provides:

```text id="qpf004"
First Page

↓

Next Page

↓

Next Page

↓

Continue
```

The user can begin working immediately while additional results remain available.

---

# Lazy Aggregation

Aggregate calculations should only occur when requested.

For example:

```text id="qpf005"
Open Character

↓

Do Not Count Every Relationship
```

Only when the user requests statistics:

```text id="qpf006"
Calculate Relationship Count
```

This avoids unnecessary work during normal navigation.

---

# Parallel Coordination

When independent work exists:

```text id="qpf007"
Node Query

Card Query

Link Query
```

the Execution Coordinator may dispatch them concurrently, respecting the execution plan.

---

# Memory Discipline

The Query Engine keeps only temporary execution data.

```text id="qpf008"
Execution

↓

Merge

↓

Return

↓

Release Memory
```

Long-term caching belongs to the engines that own the data.

---

# Result Pagination

Large collections are always paginated.

Every paginated response follows the same structure:

- Page size
- Current position
- Total available (when practical)
- Continuation information

This keeps responses predictable across the application.

---

# Query Time Monitoring

The Query Engine records execution metrics such as:

- Planning time
- Optimization time
- Execution time
- Merge time

These metrics support diagnostics and future tuning, but they are not shown to end users by default.

---

# Stable Performance

Performance should remain predictable regardless of project age.

Adding more books or worldbuilding content should not require redesigning the architecture.

Instead, existing optimization and planning mechanisms should continue to scale.

---

# Background Queries

Expensive operations may execute in the background when appropriate.

Examples:

- World statistics
- Relationship reports
- Consistency analysis
- Large cross-project searches

The user remains free to continue working while these complete.

---

# Offline Guarantee

Every performance mechanism:

- Planning
- Optimization
- Pagination
- Parallel coordination
- Monitoring

operates entirely offline.

---

# Acceptance Criteria

Performance is complete when:

- Complexity estimation exists.
- Incremental result delivery is supported.
- Lazy aggregation is defined.
- Parallel coordination is supported.
- Temporary memory usage is documented.
- Pagination is standardized.
- Execution metrics are collected.
- Background execution is supported.
- Offline performance is guaranteed.

---

# One improvement I'd like to introduce

I think we should add a **Query Budget System**.

Instead of allowing a single query to consume unlimited resources, each execution receives a configurable "budget."

Conceptually:

```text id="qpf009"
Planning Budget

↓

Execution Budget

↓

Memory Budget

↓

Result Budget
```

The budget isn't a hard failure mechanism. Rather, it guides the Execution Coordinator to:

- Prefer incremental delivery over loading everything at once.
- Switch to background execution for exceptionally large requests.
- Avoid monopolizing system resources.
- Keep the editor responsive even while complex queries are running.

This doesn't change what the query returns. It only influences *how* the work is scheduled and delivered.

## One architectural suggestion

While writing this section, I noticed another reusable pattern.

Both the **Link Engine** and the **Query Engine** now include concepts like:

- Background work
- Progress tracking
- Cancellation
- Timeouts
- Resource management

Rather than letting each engine implement these independently, I think these operational concerns should eventually become part of a shared **Execution Framework** under the Core Standards.

That framework wouldn't own querying or relationships. It would simply provide common mechanisms for long-running operations across LoreCanvas. The engines would continue to own their domain logic, but they'd all benefit from a consistent approach to execution management, reducing duplication while keeping the architecture cohesive.

I think we're slowly building what I'd call a **"Sleeping Architecture."**

Most of the system stays inactive.

Conceptually:

```text

├── Sleeping

Node Engine

├── Sleeping

Card Engine

├── Sleeping

├── Sleeping

├── Sleeping
```

- Lower RAM usage.
- Lower CPU usage.
- Better battery life.
- Fewer unnecessary background tasks.
